# Read what's yours: identity, roles, actions, and projects

In this tutorial you will learn to read "what's mine" from Glassfrog with the
`glassfrog` CLI. You will start by confirming who your token resolves to, then
progressively read the roles you fill, the actions on your plate, and the
projects you are responsible for — all without ever naming yourself, because
your stored token already scopes every call to one person in one organization.

By the end you will be able to orient yourself in Glassfrog from the command
line: prove your token works, and list the governance work that is yours.

## Prerequisites

- The `glassfrog` CLI installed and on your `PATH`.
- A configured API token. The Self-Service Reads commands identify you by your
  stored token, not by anything you type on the command line. If you have not
  set up a token yet, follow the authentication tutorial first
  (`docs/guides/authentication/tutorial.md`) and come back here once
  `glassfrog auth login` has stored your credential.

This tutorial assumes your token is already in place. It does not re-teach
authentication.

## Step 1 — Confirm who you are with `glassfrog me`

The smallest read is `me`. It is the first call to make: it proves the whole
chain works end-to-end and tells you which actor and organization your token
resolves to.

Run it with no arguments:

```
glassfrog me
```

You will see a reshaped, predictable projection — one labelled line per fact:

```
actor:        Alice Smith (human) per_0123456789abcdef0123456789abcdef
organization: Acme (org_0123456789abcdef0123456789abcdef)
access:       admin
```

That tells you three things at once: the **actor** (your name, your kind, and
your id), the **organization** you are in (name and id), and your membership
**access** level. The command exits successfully, so a script or AI agent can
tell the call worked just from the exit code.

Notice the id values (`per_…`, `org_…`). They are always present — they are the
machine-actionable handles you reuse in follow-up calls.

If your token resolves to an AI agent rather than a person, the same command
reports the actor's kind as `agent` and surfaces an `agt_` id instead:

```
actor:        Claude (agent) agt_0123456789abcdef0123456789abcdef
organization: Acme (org_0123456789abcdef0123456789abcdef)
access:       normal
```

You have now confirmed your token works and learned who and where you are.

## Step 2 — Get your roles in the same call with `--include roles`

When you are about to act on someone's behalf, it helps to see their roles in
the same round-trip. The `me` command takes an opt-in `--include roles` flag
that embeds the requester's roles in the identity read:

```
glassfrog me --include roles
```

The projection now gains a `roles` section listing each embedded role's name
and id, alongside the identity facts you already saw:

```
actor:        Claude (agent) agt_0123456789abcdef0123456789abcdef
organization: Acme (org_0123456789abcdef0123456789abcdef)
access:       normal
roles:
  - Marketing Lead (role_0123456789abcdef0123456789abcdef)
  - Treasurer (role_00000000000000000000000000000001)
```

This embed is the API's convenience affordance — a quick orientation, identity
plus a roster of role names and ids in one call. For a fuller view of each
role, move on to Step 3.

## Step 3 — List the roles you fill with `glassfrog me roles`

To read the roles you hold in detail — not just their names and ids — use the
dedicated `me roles` command:

```
glassfrog me roles
```

Each role prints as its own block, with a blank line between blocks:

```
Marketing Lead (role_0123456789abcdef0123456789abcdef)
  Purpose: <purpose>
  Domains:
    - <domain description>
    - <domain description>
  Accountabilities:
    - <accountability description>
    - <accountability description>
```

Each role shows its **name** and id on the first line, then its **Purpose**,
its **Domains**, and its **Accountabilities** (each as its description text).
The command exits successfully. This is the read half of acting on a
practitioner's behalf: see the roles you hold, then decide where to sense a
tension or raise a proposal.

If you fill no roles, that is still a clean answer — the command prints exactly
`No roles.` and exits successfully. An empty list is a valid result, not an
error.

## Step 4 — See the actions on your plate with `glassfrog me actions`

Now read the next-actions owned by the roles you fill:

```
glassfrog me actions
```

The actions projection lists one entry per action, each carrying its **id**,
**status**, **description**, and the **owning role**:

```
actn_0123456789abcdef0123456789abcdef  [current]   Review PR #6818
  role: role_0123456789abcdef0123456789abcdef   tags: marketing, q2
actn_00000000000000000000000000000001  [waiting]   Draft Q2 plan
  role: role_0123456789abcdef0123456789abcdef
```

The command exits successfully. If you own no actions, the projection prints an
explicit empty-result line (`No actions.`) rather than nothing — again, a valid
answer, not a failure.

When you want to focus on just the live work, add a status filter:

```
glassfrog me actions --status current
```

Only the actions the API returns for that status are rendered. The supported
status values are `archived`, `cancelled`, `completed`, `current`,
`scheduled`, `someday`, and `waiting`.

## Step 5 — See the projects you're responsible for with `glassfrog me projects`

The last read is the twin of the previous one, over projects instead of
actions:

```
glassfrog me projects
```

Each project prints with its **id**, **status**, **description**, and **owning
role**:

```
proj_0123456789abcdef0123456789abcdef  [current]   Rebuild onboarding flow
  role: role_0123456789abcdef0123456789abcdef   sub-projects: yes   actions: yes   tags: q2
proj_00000000000000000000000000000001  [scheduled] Audit vendor list
  role: —   sub-projects: no   actions: no
```

A project that is not owned by a role you fill renders an explicit no-role
marker (`—`) and still surfaces its id, status, and description. The same
`--status` filter works here too:

```
glassfrog me projects --status current
```

If you own no projects, the projection prints `no projects` and exits
successfully.

## What You've Learned

You have walked the whole Self-Service Reads surface:

- `glassfrog me` confirms who your token resolves to, and `me --include roles`
  embeds your roles in the same call.
- `glassfrog me roles` lists the roles you fill, each with its purpose,
  domains, and accountabilities.
- `glassfrog me actions` and `glassfrog me projects` list the actions and
  projects owned by the roles you fill, with an optional `--status` filter.

Every command identifies you by your stored token, prints a reshaped
projection to stdout, and exits successfully on a clean read — including when
the result is an empty list.

**Next steps:**

- To accomplish a specific task — list the roles, actions, and projects that
  are yours, and handle the common failure cases — see the how-to guide,
  `docs/guides/self-service-reads/how-to-list-whats-mine.md`.
- For the full command details, flags, output fields, and exit codes, see the
  reference docs: `docs/reference/identity-read.md`,
  `docs/reference/my-roles.md`, `docs/reference/my-actions.md`, and
  `docs/reference/my-projects.md`.
